verifyNote: Written from standard research methods and evidence-based practice teaching. Always check against Dr Collins's slides and the library workshop materials — terminology and preferred tests can differ.

topics.title: Research design
topics.summary: The design of a study decides what it can tell you. Experimental studies (like randomised controlled trials) can test cause and effect; observational studies (cohort, case-control, cross-sectional) describe and find associations. Bias and confounding are what you're always looking out for.
keyPoints: Hierarchy of evidence (roughly): systematic reviews/meta-analyses → RCTs → cohort → case-control → cross-sectional → case series/reports → expert opinion.
RCT: participants randomly allocated to interventions; randomisation balances known and unknown confounders.
Masking (blinding) of participants, clinicians and assessors reduces performance and detection bias.
Cohort study: follow people with and without an exposure forward in time (prospective) or using past records (retrospective).
Case-control: start with people who have the outcome and compare past exposures with controls — good for rare conditions.
Cross-sectional: a snapshot at one time point — prevalence and associations, not cause.
Bias types: selection, measurement/observer, recall, attrition; confounding is a third factor linked to both exposure and outcome.
We try to falsify the null hypothesis: a hypothesis can be disproved but never proven, and there is only one null to test against.
One-tailed hypotheses predict a direction; two-tailed predict any change.
Variables: independent (manipulated), dependent (measured), confounding (changes with the IV, which ruins the experiment) and extraneous (kept constant).
Floor and ceiling effects hide changes; pilot studies set task difficulty and doses.
Within-subjects designs remove differences between people; control order effects (learning, fatigue) by counterbalancing or randomised blocks.
examTraps: Saying a cross-sectional study shows cause.
Confusing blinding with randomisation.
Mixing up cohort (exposure → outcome) and case-control (outcome → look back at exposure).

diagram.description: Pyramid with layers from bottom to top: expert opinion; case reports/series; cross-sectional; case-control; cohort; randomised controlled trials; systematic reviews and meta-analyses at the top.

goDeeper.heading: Confounding with an eye example
goDeeper.body: A study finds children who use screens more are more myopic. But children who use screens more may also spend less time outdoors — and time outdoors is protective. Outdoor time is a potential confounder. Designs and analyses (randomisation, matching, adjustment in regression) try to deal with confounders.

goDeeper.heading: Repeatability and validity
goDeeper.body: Repeatability: does the same test give the same result when repeated under the same conditions? Validity: does it measure what it claims to? A tonometer can be highly repeatable but consistently read 3 mmHg high (precise but biased). Agreement between two instruments is assessed with Bland–Altman analysis, not correlation.

flashcards.back: To balance known and unknown confounders between groups.

Half the participants do condition A first and half do B first, so order effects cancel out.

topics.title: Descriptive and inferential statistics
topics.summary: Descriptive statistics summarise data (averages, spread); inferential statistics use a sample to draw conclusions about a population (confidence intervals, p-values, hypothesis tests). Choosing the right test depends on the data type, distribution and whether groups are paired.
keyPoints: Central tendency: mean (normal data), median (skewed data), mode.
Spread: standard deviation (normal data), interquartile range (skewed data).
Normal distribution: about 68% within ±1 SD, 95% within ±1.96 SD, 99.7% within ±3 SD.
Standard error = SD ÷ √n; a 95% confidence interval ≈ mean ± 1.96 × SE.
p-value: the probability of results at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true; commonly significant if p < 0.05.
Type I error = false positive (α); type II error = false negative (β); power = 1 − β.
Common tests: paired/unpaired t-test (normal data), Wilcoxon signed-rank / Mann–Whitney U (non-parametric), chi-squared (categorical), ANOVA (3+ groups), Pearson/Spearman correlation.
SE = SD ÷ √n; graphs of means usually show ±1 SE error bars.
p is the probability of results at least this extreme if H0 were true. p ≤ 0.05 significant, p ≤ 0.01 highly significant; we 'have evidence for' H1 but haven't proven it.
Statistical significance isn't the same as clinical importance.
Choose one- or two-tailed in advance (registered reports enforce this). Use a t-test for two conditions, ANOVA for more.
examTraps: Saying p = 0.03 means a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true.
Using a parametric test on clearly skewed data.
Treating 'not significant' as 'no difference' (it may be underpowered).

diagram.description: Bell-shaped normal distribution with the mean at the centre and shaded bands at ±1 SD (68%), ±2 SD (95%) and ±3 SD (99.7%).

goDeeper.heading: Choosing a test
goDeeper.body: Ask: What type of data (continuous, ordinal, categorical)? Is it normally distributed? How many groups? Are the measurements paired (same people twice, or two eyes of one person) or independent? E.g. IOP before and after a drop in the same people, normal data → paired t-test; VA (often skewed) in two separate groups → Mann–Whitney U.

goDeeper.heading: Sensitivity and specificity
goDeeper.body: Sensitivity: proportion of people with the disease that the test correctly flags (true positive rate). Specificity: proportion without the disease correctly cleared (true negative rate). Positive predictive value depends on how common the disease is — screening tests for rare conditions produce many false positives even with good specificity.

goDeeper.heading: Confidence intervals over p-values
goDeeper.body: A confidence interval shows the size and precision of an effect: 'myopia progression slowed by 0.30 D (95% CI 0.18 to 0.42)' tells you much more than 'p < 0.001'. If a 95% CI for a difference crosses zero, the result isn't significant at the 5% level.

flashcards.back: SE = SD ÷ √n.
False positive (rejecting a true null hypothesis).

topics.title: Reading and critiquing a paper
topics.summary: Critical appraisal means judging whether a study's results are trustworthy and useful. Use a structured checklist (such as CASP) and work through the question, design, methods, results and how far you can apply them to your patients.
keyPoints: Papers usually follow IMRaD: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion.
Is there a clear, focused question (PICO: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome)?
Is the design appropriate for the question?
Methods: how were participants selected? Randomised? Masked? Was follow-up complete?
Results: how big is the effect and how precise (confidence intervals)? Is it clinically meaningful, not just statistically significant?
Applicability: are the participants like your patients? Are the outcomes relevant?
Check funding, conflicts of interest, peer review and the journal's credibility.
examTraps: Appraising from the abstract alone.
Equating statistical significance with clinical importance.
Ignoring dropouts and loss to follow-up.

diagram.description: A paper shaped like an hourglass: broad Introduction narrowing to the specific question, Methods and Results in the narrow middle, Discussion widening back out to implications. Side notes list appraisal questions for each part.

goDeeper.heading: Clinical vs statistical significance
goDeeper.body: A huge study can find a 'significant' IOP difference of 0.3 mmHg that makes no difference to patients. A small study may find a large, important effect that isn't statistically significant because it's underpowered. Look at the effect size and its confidence interval, and ask whether it would change what you do.

goDeeper.heading: Spotting weak evidence
goDeeper.body: Warning signs: no control group, outcomes chosen after seeing the data, large dropouts, small samples with big claims, results only reported as p-values, industry funding with no independent replication, or conclusions that go beyond the data.

flashcards.back: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion.
Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome.

flashcards.front: A widely used UK appraisal checklist
flashcards.back: CASP (Critical Appraisal Skills Programme).

flashcards.front: What shows size and precision of an effect?
flashcards.back: The effect size with its confidence interval.

options.text: A major clinical breakthrough
options.feedback: Large samples can make tiny effects significant.

options.text: Not trustworthy because it's significant

mcq.explanation: Statistical significance tells you the effect probably isn't zero, not that it matters clinically.

topics.title: Evidence-based practice
topics.summary: Evidence-based practice means combining the best available research with your clinical expertise and the patient's values and circumstances. Guidelines (NICE, College CMGs) do much of the evidence-gathering for you, but you still need to apply them thoughtfully.
keyPoints: Definition (after Sackett): integrating best research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values.
Five steps: Ask (a focused question), Acquire (search), Appraise, Apply, Assess (evaluate the outcome).
Frame questions with PICO.
Use pre-appraised sources first: guidelines, systematic reviews (e.g. Cochrane), College CMGs.
Patient values matter: the best treatment on paper may not suit a patient's life, budget or preferences.
Evidence changes — keep up to date through CPD.
Audit your own practice: are you doing what the evidence and guidelines say?
examTraps: Defining EBP as 'just following research'.
Ignoring patient preferences.
Relying on a single study when a systematic review exists.

diagram.description: Three overlapping circles: best research evidence, clinical expertise, patient values and preferences. The overlap in the middle is labelled evidence-based practice.

goDeeper.heading: A PICO example
goDeeper.body: P: children aged 6–12 with progressing myopia. I: myopia-control spectacle lenses. C: single vision spectacles. O: change in axial length over 2 years. Turning a vague question ('do these lenses work?') into PICO makes searching and appraising much easier.

goDeeper.heading: Guidelines in UK optometry
goDeeper.body: NICE guidelines (e.g. NG81 for glaucoma) and the College of Optometrists' Clinical Management Guidelines bring the evidence together for common conditions. Use them as your default, record when and why you depart from them, and check the date — guidelines are updated.

flashcards.back: Research evidence, clinical expertise, patient values.
Ask, Acquire, Appraise, Apply, Assess.
The Cochrane Library.
College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines.

mcq.explanation: Start with high-quality pre-appraised sources (guidelines, systematic reviews) before individual studies.

topics.title: Using the library and literature search
topics.summary: A good search is planned: break your question into concepts, list synonyms, combine them with Boolean operators, and use the right databases and filters. Keep a record of what you searched so it's reproducible. The library workshop (with Giada Zanella) is your chance to practise.
keyPoints: Databases: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library; Google Scholar for a broad sweep.
Break the question into concepts (e.g. PICO) and list synonyms and spelling variants for each.
Boolean: OR within a concept (widens), AND between concepts (narrows), NOT to exclude (use carefully).
Truncation (e.g. myop* finds myopia, myopic) and phrase searching ("contact lens").
Subject headings (MeSH in PubMed) catch papers that use different words.
Filters: date, language, study type, humans.
Use a reference manager and the referencing style your module asks for; record your search strategy.
Library method: split the question into concepts, brainstorm synonyms, join synonyms with OR and concepts with AND, then filter by date and language.
examTraps: Searching one keyword in Google and stopping there.
Using AND between synonyms (narrows instead of widening).
Not recording the search, so it can't be repeated or described in your methods.

diagram.description: Venn diagrams: 'myopia OR nearsightedness' (both circles shaded — wider), 'myopia AND children' (only the overlap shaded — narrower), 'myopia NOT adults' (one circle shaded minus the overlap).

goDeeper.heading: Building a search string
goDeeper.body: Question: does orthokeratology slow myopia in children? Concepts: orthokeratology; myopia; children. String: (orthokeratology OR ortho-k OR "corneal reshaping") AND (myop* OR nearsighted*) AND (child* OR paediatric OR pediatric). Add filters for systematic reviews or RCTs if you want the strongest evidence first.

goDeeper.heading: Judging sources
goDeeper.body: Prefer peer-reviewed journals and established databases. Be wary of predatory journals (aggressive emails, very fast acceptance, unclear peer review). Check who wrote and funded a piece. Professional magazines (e.g. Optometry Today) are useful for clinical updates but aren't primary research.

flashcards.back: OR widens (synonyms); AND narrows (combines concepts).
myop* → myopia, myopic, myopes.
MeSH (Medical Subject Headings).
So it's reproducible and can be reported in your methods.

flashcards.back: A primary paper (no reviews), within the date limit and at least 4 pages long.

topics.title: The retina, LGN and visual pathways
topics.summary: How light becomes a neural signal and gets to the cortex. The retina is wired back to front, trades sensitivity against resolution through convergence, and sends its output mainly through the LGN to V1.
keyPoints: Visible light spans about 380 to 760 nm. Wavelength goes with hue, amplitude with brightness, purity with saturation. Light itself is not coloured.
Receptors hyperpolarise to light with graded potentials. Retinal ganglion cells are the first cells to fire action potentials.
About 120 million rods and 8 million cones per retina, but only about 1 million optic nerve fibres: average convergence 100:1.
Convergence is low in the fovea (good resolution) and high in the periphery (good sensitivity): a duplex system.
P-cells (about 80%): small, slow, small receptive fields, wavelength-sensitive. M-cells (about 10%): large, fast, large fields, flicker-sensitive, high contrast sensitivity.
Primary pathway: retina, chiasm, tract, LGN, optic radiation, layer 4C of V1. It carries about 90% of retinal output and each hemifield goes to the opposite hemisphere.
LGN: 6 layers. Top 4 parvocellular, bottom 2 magnocellular, koniocellular cells between. Only about 10% of its input is retinal.
examTraps: Saying the central fovea has all three cone classes. It has no blue cones (and no rods).
Treating the upside-down map in V1 as a problem the brain has to correct. It isn't one.
Calling the LGN just a relay. Most of its input is feedback from cortex and elsewhere, so it probably regulates the signal.

goDeeper.heading: Purkinje shift
goDeeper.body: Rods are most sensitive near 500 nm (blue-green) and cones near 550 nm (yellow). In daylight yellow flowers look lighter than green leaves; as night falls and rods take over, the leaves start to look lighter.

goDeeper.heading: The blind spot and filling in
goDeeper.body: The optic disc, 12 to 18° from the fovea, has no receptors. Each eye's blind spot is on the nasal retina so the two don't overlap, but even with one eye closed you see no hole because the visual system fills in from the surround. Something similar happens for blue in the central fovea: a tiny pure blue spot seen from far away looks black.

goDeeper.heading: Afterimages and size constancy
goDeeper.body: An afterimage has a fixed size on the retina, yet it looks larger when you look at a far wall than at a near sheet of paper. The visual system scales perceived size by perceived distance.

goDeeper.heading: Names for primary visual cortex
goDeeper.body: V1, striate cortex (for the visible stripe of myelinated axons), Brodmann's area 17, and calcarine cortex in clinical writing (much of it lies in the calcarine sulcus). The fovea is represented at the occipital pole.

flashcards.back: About 100 receptors to 1 ganglion cell. Lower in the fovea, higher in the periphery.

flashcards.front: Which retinal cells fire action potentials?
flashcards.back: Retinal ganglion cells. Receptors and most interneurons use graded potentials.
Six: top four parvocellular, bottom two magnocellular, koniocellular cells in between. Each layer takes input from one eye.
To the superior colliculus (midbrain) and to the pulvinar (thalamus).
The region of retina which, when stimulated, changes a cell's response (up or down).

flashcards.front: Size of the fovea and its rod-free centre
flashcards.back: Fovea 1.5 mm (5.2°); rod-free region 0.5 mm (1.7°).

cases.scenario: A friend says that because the image on the retina and the map in V1 are upside down, the brain must flip it the right way up.
cases.question: How would you answer using this lecture?
cases.modelAnswer: The cortical 'image' is not a picture that anything looks at; it is a pattern of neural activity. What matters is that the mapping is orderly (retinotopic), not which way up it is. So the inversion presents no computational problem to solve.

topics.title: Receptive fields and convolution
topics.summary: A receptive field is a weighting function. When an array of cells applies the same weighting function across the whole image (convolution), the output is a neural image that marks edges, discards uniform areas, and exists at several spatial scales.
keyPoints: Receptive field: the region of retina which, when stimulated, changes the cell's response (up or down).
On-centre cells have an excitatory centre and inhibitory surround; off-centre the reverse. There are roughly equal numbers of each, and fields grow with eccentricity.
Response = light on excitatory regions minus light on inhibitory regions. With uniform light these cancel, leaving the spontaneous rate.
Responses: spontaneous discharge, a transient (phasic) burst at onset, then a sustained (tonic, steady-state) level.
Convolution: at every position multiply the image by the weighting function and sum. Convolving is a form of filtering.
Edges show up as zero-crossings in the neural image; uniform areas are discarded, which is data compression.
Different information sits at different spatial scales, so the retina produces overlapping neural images at several scales.
examTraps: Saying a receptive field is a region of the brain. It is a region of the retina (or visual field).
Thinking a centre-surround cell responds to uniform light. It responds only to a change in luminance within its field.
Confusing the steady-state (sustained) response with spontaneous discharge, which is the rate with no stimulus.

goDeeper.heading: Why the Hermann grid shows blobs
goDeeper.body: An on-centre cell centred on an intersection has light falling on more of its inhibitory surround (four arms) than one centred on a bar (two arms), so it responds less and signals less lightness. The blobs disappear at the intersection you look straight at, where fields are small.

goDeeper.heading: Negative numbers in neurons
goDeeper.body: Convolution with a centre-surround kernel produces positive and negative values. Neurons can't fire negatively, so spontaneous discharge acts as zero, and the on- and off-centre systems carry the two halves: two complementary neural images.

flashcards.back: Slide a weighting function (kernel) across the image; at each position multiply and sum to give one output value. The result is the neural image.

flashcards.front: Where is an edge in the neural image?
flashcards.back: At the zero-crossing between above- and below-spontaneous responses.

flashcards.front: Three jobs ganglion cells do by convolution
flashcards.back: Analyse at several spatial scales, highlight edges, and remove redundancy (compress data).

flashcards.front: Effect of widening a Gaussian weighting function
flashcards.back: More blur: fine detail is filtered out.

cases.scenario: An array of on-centre ganglion cells views a vertical edge, light on the left and dark on the right.
cases.question: Describe the response of cells across the array and explain each part.
cases.modelAnswer: Far left (all light) and far right (all dark): spontaneous rate, because centre and surround cancel or neither is stimulated. A cell centred exactly on the edge: also spontaneous, as centre and surround get equal light. Just left of the edge: the centre is fully lit but part of the surround is dark, so less inhibition and a response above spontaneous. Just right of the edge: the centre is dark but part of the surround is lit, so the response falls below spontaneous. The edge is marked by the zero-crossing between these, and the uniform areas carry no extra signal.

topics.title: Primary visual cortex (V1)
topics.summary: V1 turns the retina's centre-surround code into orientation-selective responses, organised into modules that each analyse one small patch of the visual field for orientation, eye of origin and colour.
keyPoints: Retinotopic but distorted: about half of V1 represents the central 10° of the visual field.
V1 is the first stage with orientation selectivity. Most cortical cells have little or no background firing.
Simple cells: elongated, separate excitatory and inhibitory regions; selective for orientation, size and position (phase).
Complex cells: no separate on and off regions; orientation- and size-selective but respond anywhere in the field; non-linear; like moving or flickering stimuli.
End-stopping (once called 'hypercomplex') prefers contours that end in the field and occurs in simple and complex cells.
Orientation columns make up a hypercolumn covering all orientations at one location. Population responses, not single cells, code orientation; the tilt aftereffect is evidence.
Ocular dominance columns alternate between the eyes; cytochrome oxidase blobs at their centres hold colour-selective (double-opponent) cells. About 2,500 modules of about 100,000 cells.
examTraps: Calling simple cells 'edge detectors': they respond to bars of either polarity too, so their response is ambiguous.
Thinking one cell's firing tells you orientation. Contrast and orientation are confounded; you need the population.
Saying blob cells are sharply orientation-tuned. They are broadly tuned or untuned.

goDeeper.heading: How the maps were found
goDeeper.body: 2-deoxyglucose is taken up by active cells, so after showing an animal a stimulus, autoradiography of cortical slices reveals which cells responded: this gave the retinotopic map (Tootell et al., 1982). Injecting a tracer into one eye gives alternating stripes: ocular dominance columns (LeVay et al., 1975). Staining for cytochrome oxidase, a metabolic enzyme, reveals the blobs (Tootell et al., 1983). Optical imaging later confirmed and extended these maps.

goDeeper.heading: The tilt aftereffect as a population code
goDeeper.body: Stare at a tilted grating and the cells tuned to that tilt get tired. A vertical test pattern then excites a population whose peak is pushed away from the adapted orientation, so vertical looks tilted the other way. A system of single feature detectors would predict no such shift.

flashcards.back: Simple: separate on and off regions, sensitive to exact position. Complex: no separate regions, responds to the right orientation and size anywhere in its field.
A group of V1 orientation columns that together cover all orientations for roughly the same part of the visual field.

flashcards.front: How are ocular dominance columns revealed?
flashcards.back: Inject a radioactive tracer into one eye and autoradiograph V1: alternating labelled and unlabelled stripes.
Cytochrome-oxidase-rich patches in the centres of ocular dominance columns: colour-selective, low spatial frequency, poorly tuned for orientation.

topics.title: Beyond V1: the ventral ('what') stream
topics.summary: After V1, vision splits into specialised areas and two broad streams. The ventral stream (V1 to V2 to V4 to IT) builds up the representation of form, colour and objects, and damage to it causes specific agnosias.
keyPoints: Over 30 visual areas with over 300 connections. Moving up, receptive fields grow, maps get cruder and selectivity becomes more complex; there is feedback throughout.
Two streams (Ungerleider and Mishkin): ventral 'what' to the temporal lobe (IT), dorsal 'where' to the parietal lobe (e.g. area 7a).
Evidence: retrograde tracers in parietal and temporal cortex label almost separate cells earlier on (Baizer et al., 1991); parietal damage gives Balint's syndrome, temporal damage gives agnosia.
V2: cytochrome oxidase thick stripes (stereo), thin stripes (colour) and interstripes (form). Many V2 cells respond to illusory contours; V1 cells don't.
V4: crude map, colour columns (globs), some colour constancy, and cells tuned to curves. Damage causes achromatopsia.
IT: 'elaborate' cells for combinations of features, and face-selective cells; a face is probably coded by about 100 cells together.
examTraps: Calling face cells 'grandmother cells'. Each responds to many faces; identity is in the population.
Taking prosopagnosia as proof of a face area without a fair within-class comparison (e.g. a farmer recognising individual cows).
Saying all V4 cells are colour blind, or that V4 does only colour.

goDeeper.heading: Seven clinical conditions
goDeeper.body: Cortical blindness (V1 damage), blindsight (responding to things not consciously seen), optic ataxia (trouble reaching), ocular apraxia (trouble directing the eyes), simultanagnosia (seeing only one object at a time); the last three together make Balint's syndrome. Visual agnosia (failing to recognise objects) and prosopagnosia (faces) come from temporal damage; achromatopsia (colour loss with form preserved) from V4 damage.

goDeeper.heading: Illusory contours in V2
goDeeper.body: Peterhans and von der Heydt drifted Kanizsa-type figures across V2 receptive fields. Cells fired to real edges and to illusory edges, but not when the 'pac-men' gaps were closed or only half the figure was shown. Because the response tracks the perception, the contour may be built bottom-up in V2 rather than only inferred by higher areas.

flashcards.back: Optic ataxia, ocular apraxia and simultanagnosia, after parietal (dorsal stream) damage.
Thin stripes: colour (from V1 blobs). Thick stripes: stereo. Interstripes: form (from V1 interblobs).
Complete loss of colour vision with form preserved: V4 damage.
IT cells that respond to particular combinations of complex spatial features (Tanaka, 1993).

topics.title: Beyond V1: the dorsal ('where'/'action') stream
topics.summary: The parietal route from V1 through MT and MST to area 7a analyses motion and space, and may be better thought of as guiding action than locating objects.
keyPoints: MT (V5): receptive fields of 5–10°, columns for direction of motion, sensitivity to relative motion, depth from motion and disparity.
V1 codes the separate components of a plaid; MT 'pattern cells' code the overall motion we actually perceive.
Akinetopsia (motion blindness) follows damage to MT on both sides.
MST: fields of 30–50°, tuned to expansion, contraction, rotation and spirals, as in optic flow during self-motion.
Coordinate frames: retinocentric, egocentric and allocentric. 7a has gaze-locked cells; PO has 'real position' cells whose fields aren't fixed on the retina.
Zeki: four pathways (motion, colour, form with colour, form without colour), with cross-talk; V3 doesn't fit what/where.
Milner and Goodale: ventral = perception, dorsal = action. DF (ventral damage) could post a card through a slot but couldn't report its orientation; optic ataxia (dorsal damage) is the reverse.
examTraps: Saying the dorsal stream simply handles moving objects and the ventral stream stationary ones.
Giving DF's damage as dorsal: it was ventral (visual form agnosia).
Treating blindsight as evidence that V1 is where seeing happens: it shows V1 is needed for awareness, not that awareness happens there.

goDeeper.heading: Population coding capacity
goDeeper.body: Four cells, each with five distinguishable response levels, can in principle signal 5 × 5 × 5 × 5 = 625 different combinations. That is why about 100 face cells could code a very large number of faces.

goDeeper.heading: Perception versus action in healthy people
goDeeper.body: Aglioti et al. (1995) reported that grip aperture wasn't fooled by the Titchener (Ebbinghaus) size illusion even though perception was, which fits the action/perception split. Franz et al. (2000) couldn't replicate it, and Haffenden and Goodale (2000) disputed their stimuli. The question is still open.

flashcards.back: Motion blindness: seeing the world as a series of snapshots. Needs damage to MT on both sides.
The pattern of motion on the retina as we move (expansion moving forward, rotation turning the head); MST cells are tuned to these patterns.
Egocentric: position relative to yourself. Allocentric: position relative to other objects or the room.
M cells, then V1 layer 4B (and V2 thick stripes), then MT.

topics.title: Perceptual grouping and visual search
topics.summary: Mid-level vision links local features into surfaces and objects. The Gestalt rules describe how elements group, figure-ground segregation separates objects from backgrounds, and visual search experiments show which features the brain codes in parallel.
keyPoints: Gestalt rules: proximity, similarity, good continuation, closure, symmetry, common fate (elements moving together group).
Prägnanz ('good figure'): we see the simplest structure possible, but simplicity is hard to define or compute.
Rules compete with no fixed order: proximity can beat similarity or lose to it.
Figure-ground: border-ownership cells in V2 help decide which side of an edge is the object.
Contour linking: smooth chains of aligned elements are easy to see, which suggests an 'association field' in V1/V2.
Feature search is parallel (pop-out; reaction time flat as distractors increase); conjunction search is serial (reaction time rises).
Enns and Rensink (1990): search can be parallel for 3D orientation, so grouping uses depth and Marr's strictly feed-forward stages can't be right.
examTraps: Saying the Gestalt rules explain grouping: they describe it.
Assuming pop-out only reflects V1 features.

goDeeper.heading: Running a visual search experiment
goDeeper.body: Measure reaction time to find a target among different numbers of distractors. A flat line means parallel search (the target pops out); a line rising with each extra distractor means serial search, item by item.

flashcards.back: Elements that move together are grouped together.
The 'law of good figure': every pattern is seen as the simplest structure possible.
Finding a target defined by two features (e.g. green and horizontal) among distractors sharing one; reaction time rises with the number of distractors.
2D image features, then surfaces, then 3D objects, in a strictly feed-forward sequence.

mcq.q: A shape only becomes visible when it moves relative to its background. This is grouping by

options.text: common fate
proximity
closure
similarity
options.feedback: That's about shared features such as colour.

options.text: good continuation

options.text: contributes to figure-ground segregation
options.feedback: Yes: it signals which side of an edge belongs to the figure.

topics.title: Lightness perception
topics.summary: We perceive the lightness of surfaces (reflectance), not the amount of light reaching the eye. The visual system recovers reflectance from luminance ratios at edges, anchoring, and its interpretation of shadows and 3D layout.
keyPoints: L = I × r (luminance = illuminance × reflectance). The retina receives only L.
Lightness refers to surfaces; brightness refers to light. Lightness constancy: surfaces look the same under different illumination.
The ratio of neighbouring luminances equals the ratio of their reflectances, whatever the illumination.
Anchoring: assume the lightest region is white to turn relative values into absolute lightness.
Ganglion cells respond strongly to sharp luminance changes and weakly to gradual ones, which explains the Craik-O'Brien-Cornsweet illusion and lightness contrast.
Fuzzy shadow edges (penumbras) aren't treated as reflectance changes; perceived 3D layout can change perceived lightness (Adelson) and the reverse (crater/volcano).
examTraps: Calling lightness a physical quantity: it's psychological. Luminance, illuminance and reflectance are physical.
Writing L = r ÷ I instead of L = I × r.

flashcards.back: I × r: luminance = illuminance × reflectance.
Lightness: perceived reflectance of a surface. Brightness: perceived intensity of light.
Assuming the lightest region in view is white, so other greys can be scaled from it.
